hypothesis.source: arXiv:1603.02754 (Chen & Guestrin, XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System), regularized objective with column subsampling and L1/L2 leaf penalties
hypothesis.predicted_effect: val_top1_err falls from about 13.3 to about 12.6 (range 12.2-13.1) at the default lr, epochs and model size.

reasoning.trace: The ledger is empty: there are no runs, no warnings and no frontier. The campaign exists to test the XGBoost-transfer idea, so the first step is a clean treatment that holds the config at the defaults (the 13.3 baseline recipe). That way the implicit control is the unmodified script with the identical config. The idea's main claim is that most of the gain comes from vocabulary-column subsampling, so this treatment implements the two core mechanisms through a train-script edit. The first is a fresh per-step mask that drops a fraction p=0.25 of vocabulary ids, mapping them to padding id 0 before the embedding pooling. The second is a group-L1 penalty: a sum of row L2 norms on the embedding, excluding the padding row, with coefficient 1e-5. I leave the shrinkage/EMA schedule out so that later ablations can attribute the effect. Rows that would become fully masked keep their original ids, so pooling never divides by zero. The architecture, the artifact format and the scorer interface are unchanged. I aim for 2-3 seeds to match the planned 3-seed comparison.

It also isolates those two mechanisms against an identical-config control, so it is worth running as the campaign's first step. The weak point is the setting. At embed_dim 64, 8 epochs, wd 1e-4 and 13.3% error, the model may not be overfitting much, and a group-L1 of 1e-5 is probably too small to matter. A null result would then say little about the transfer idea. Log the train/val gap and the fraction of near-zero embedding rows so a null can be read properly. If column dropout shows any signal, follow up with a bolder sweep: p in {0.1, 0.4}, λ about 1e-4, and EMA shrinkage. The ledger is empty, so a gain can only be credited if the unmodified script runs alongside this treatment on the same seeds; the 13.3 baseline alone won't do, and 2 seeds probably can't resolve a 0.6 delta, so commit to 3. hypothesis.claim: XGBoost-style shrinkage, transferred as EMA/Polyak weight averaging, further reduces val error on top of vocabulary-column subsampling (p=0.4). The mechanism is smoothing the noisy late-training iterates that column dropout induces, which should mostly help high-variance seeds such as seed 4. Config and column-dropout rate are held fixed.
hypothesis.source: arXiv:1603.02754 (Chen & Guestrin, XGBoost: shrinkage as a regularizer alongside column subsampling); Polyak & Juditsky 1992, Acceleration of stochastic approximation by averaging (SIAM J. Control Optim.)
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Full-fidelity val_top1_err of about 12.35, versus 12.55 for the frontier. The largest improvement should be on the worst seed (13.8), with seed-to-seed spread narrowing.

reasoning.trace: Ablations so far settle the column-subsampling part of the idea. On matched seeds 0-2 at the same config, vocabulary-column dropout p=0.4 with no group-L1 scored 12.08 (exp_0013), against 13.77 for the no-regularizer control (exp_0015), a gap of about 1.7 points. Adding group-L1 at 1e-6 changed nothing (12.10 in exp_0011 vs 12.08). The frontier is 12.55 on the full 5 seeds; seed 4 is an outlier at 13.8, which points to high-variance final iterates. The third XGBoost mechanism, shrinkage via weight averaging, has never been tested in isolation. It was only bundled with higher capacity, depth 2, lr 1.5e-3 and 16 epochs (exp_0006/0007), and that bundle was confounded and worse. Following the one-knob-per-experiment lesson, this run keeps the frontier code and config fixed (lr 3e-3, 64/64, depth 1, wd 1e-4, 8 epochs, COL_DROP=0.4, L1=0). The only change is EMA weight averaging, and the EMA weights are what gets saved. The decay follows a warmup schedule, min(0.999, (1+t)/(10+t)), so that a short run is not biased toward the initialisation. The comparison is paired against exp_0013/exp_0014 on the same seeds.

priors: XGBoost-style column subsampling and L1 shrinkage transferred to neural BoW (arXiv:1603.02754)

If EMA wins, the bolder follow-up is SWA-style averaging with a cyclical or constant LR tail, which directly targets the variance on seed 4.

Also log the total optimizer steps: if 8 epochs is only a few thousand steps, a 0.999 decay averages over roughly 1000 steps. That window may still be dominated by mid-training weights and could hurt rather than help, so a lower cap such as 0.99 may be needed.

Evaluate both the raw and the EMA weights in the same run on all 5 seeds, giving a within-run paired delta. Also log the total optimizer steps. If 8 epochs is only a few hundred steps, decay capped at 0.999 (about a 1000-step window) mostly averages early iterates rather than smoothing the late ones. In that case a null result would reflect lag, not a refutation of shrinkage.

hypothesis.claim: Adding row-wise group-L1 (coefficient 1e-4) on the embedding rows active in each batch, the neural analogue of XGBoost's L1 leaf-weight penalty, lowers val_top1_err relative to the column-subsampling + shrinkage frontier at identical config and seeds. hypothesis.source: arXiv:1603.02754 (Chen & Guestrin, XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System), L1 regularization on leaf weights combined with column subsampling and shrinkage for sparse high-dimensional inputs
hypothesis.predicted_effect: val_top1_err about 11.75 (range 11.5-12.1) vs 11.89 for the frontier. The paired delta is about -0.1, which is within seed noise. If the result lands above 12.0, L1 contributes nothing beyond column dropout, which supports the idea's claim that column subsampling carries most of the gain.

reasoning.trace: The frontier, exp_0022, scores 11.89 over 5 seeds. It combines column subsampling at p=0.4 with the shrinkage bundle (lr 1.5e-3, 16 epochs, EMA 0.999), and group-L1 is off. The idea under test has three components. Column subsampling has been isolated: exp_0014 gave 12.55, against 13.77 with no regularizers in exp_0015. Shrinkage/EMA has been partly isolated: EMA alone at 8 epochs gave 12.03. Group-L1 on embedding rows is the remaining component and has never been tested alone against a matched parent. Following the skill-library lesson to change one knob per experiment, this run keeps the frontier code and config identical and only enables group-L1 at 1e-4, the top of the planned grid. I chose 1e-4 over 1e-6 or 1e-5 because small values would sit far below seed noise and could not be ranked. One implementation choice matters. With Adam, a dense L1 penalty on all ~vocab rows every step gets normalized per parameter. That would drive every rare-word row toward zero at roughly lr per step whatever the coefficient, which is not XGBoost's leaf penalty. So the penalty is applied lazily, only to the embedding rows of tokens present in the current column-subsampled batch, mirroring how XGBoost only penalizes leaves that are used. The control for this pair is exp_0022, with the same code minus L1 and the same seeds.

votes.concern: This is a clean one-knob ablation that completes the decomposition of the literature-backed bundle, but it is timid. It predicts only -0.1 on a frontier where seed noise across 5 seeds is probably comparable, so a null result tells us little. The lazy per-batch penalty also departs from XGBoost's leaf penalty in a way that matters: it penalizes frequent rows more often than rare ones, which is the opposite of the stated mechanism of shrinking rare-word embeddings. It is still worth a run because it is the one untested component and is cheap. A bolder follow-up would be frequency-scaled L1, or a proximal/AdamW-style decoupled group-L1 that actually zeros rare rows, paired with a sweep of column subsampling p, since subsampling is where the large gains came from.

Those rows then still get pushed about lr toward zero each time they appear, regardless of the 1e-4 coefficient. Shrinkage has also been tested. EMA at the default schedule gave 12.03 (full), and adding lr/2 with 2x epochs gave 11.89 (full, frontier exp_0022). The only group-L1 evidence is the early combined run (12.69). That run changed several knobs at once and its config did not record them, so per the skill-library lessons it supports no conclusion. This experiment changes one thing against the frontier: GROUP_L1=1e-5, the upper end of the idea's 1e-6 to 1e-5 range. Code, col-drop rate, EMA and config are otherwise identical, and the seeds match, so the pairing is direct. The effect may be larger than the coefficient suggests. Adam rescales the constant L1 subgradient that rare-word rows receive between their sparse CE updates, so those rows shrink toward zero at roughly lr per step, while frequent-word rows are dominated by the CE gradient. That rare-word shrinkage is the leaf-L1 analogue in XGBoost. The effect may well be smaller than the roughly 0.8pt seed spread, so a null result is informative here. It would indicate that col-drop, not L1, carries the gain, as the idea predicts.

hypothesis.claim: Adding row-wise group-L1 (coefficient 1e-4) on the embedding rows active in each batch, the neural analogue of XGBoost's L1 leaf-weight penalty, lowers val_top1_err relative to the column-subsampling + shrinkage frontier at identical config and seeds. It does so by shrinking noisy rare-word embeddings, and the gain should be small compared with what column subsampling contributed.
hypothesis.source: arXiv:1603.02754 (Chen & Guestrin, XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System), L1 regularization on leaf weights combined with column subsampling and shrinkage for sparse high-dimensional inputs
hypothesis.predicted_effect: val_top1_err about 11.75 (range 11.5-12.1) vs 11.89 for the frontier. The paired delta is about -0.1, which is within seed noise. If the result lands above 12.0, L1 contributes nothing beyond column dropout, which supports the idea's claim that column subsampling carries most of the gain.

reasoning.trace: The frontier, exp_0022, scores 11.89 over 5 seeds. It combines column subsampling at p=0.4 with the shrinkage bundle (lr 1.5e-3, 16 epochs, EMA 0.999), and group-L1 is off. The idea under test has three components. Column subsampling has been isolated: exp_0014 gave 12.55, against 13.77 with no regularizers in exp_0015. Shrinkage/EMA has been partly isolated: EMA alone at 8 epochs gave 12.03. Group-L1 on embedding rows is the remaining component and has never been tested alone against a matched parent. Following the skill-library lesson to change one knob per experiment, this run keeps the frontier code and config identical and only enables group-L1 at 1e-4, the top of the planned grid. I chose 1e-4 over 1e-6 or 1e-5 because small values would sit far below seed noise and could not be ranked. One implementation choice matters. With Adam, a dense L1 penalty on all ~vocab rows every step gets normalized per parameter. That would drive every rare-word row toward zero at roughly lr per step whatever the coefficient, which is not XGBoost's leaf penalty. So the penalty is applied lazily, only to the embedding rows of tokens present in the current column-subsampled batch, mirroring how XGBoost only penalizes leaves that are used. The control for this pair is exp_0022, with the same code minus L1 and the same seeds.

priors: XGBoost-style column subsampling and L1 shrinkage transferred to neural BoW (arXiv:1603.02754)

votes.concern: This is a clean one-knob ablation that completes the decomposition of the literature-backed bundle, but it is timid. It predicts only -0.1 on a frontier where seed noise across 5 seeds is probably comparable, so a null result tells us little. The lazy per-batch penalty also departs from XGBoost's leaf penalty in a way that matters: it penalizes frequent rows more often than rare ones, which is the opposite of the stated mechanism of shrinking rare-word embeddings. It is still worth a run because it is the one untested component and is cheap. A bolder follow-up would be frequency-scaled L1, or a proximal/AdamW-style decoupled group-L1 that actually zeros rare rows, paired with a sweep of column subsampling p, since subsampling is where the large gains came from.

This is a clean single-knob ablation against a matched parent (exp_0022, same seeds), so it is cheap and well-controlled. The predicted -0.1 on 11.89, though, is likely at or below 5-seed noise. Report paired per-seed deltas and the seed std, or the result will be uninterpretable. Also confirm the lazy L1 term is still on the same scale as the data gradient under Adam for rare rows. Otherwise the sign-normalization issue just reappears on the active rows.

This is a clean one-knob ablation and worth the GPU, but the premise may be shakier than it looks. The config already applies weight_decay 1e-4 to the embeddings, so 'group-L1 shrinks noisy rare rows' mostly duplicates shrinkage that is already on. The lazy-penalty fix also doesn't fully escape Adam normalization. For rare tokens the data gradient is tiny, so the w/||w|| group term can dominate the sparse second-moment estimate. Those rows then still get pushed about lr toward zero each time they appear, regardless of the 1e-4 coefficient. Before attributing any change to the XGBoost analogy, report exp_0022's seed std, since the predicted -0.1 may sit inside it. Also log the embedding-row norm distribution by token frequency, to show whether rare-row shrinkage is actually what moved the score.

hypothesis.claim: At matched compute (lr 0.0015, 16 epochs, column subsampling p=0.4, no group-L1), removing EMA/Polyak averaging raises val_top1_err relative to the frontier. This would show that the averaging part of XGBoost-style shrinkage, not just the longer low-lr schedule, produces the 12.55 to 11.89 gain.
hypothesis.source: arXiv:1603.02754 (Chen & Guestrin, XGBoost: shrinkage as a regularizer alongside column subsampling); Polyak & Juditsky 1992, Acceleration of stochastic approximation by averaging, SIAM J. Control Optim.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: val_top1_err of about 12.3 (range 12.0-12.6), roughly +0.4 versus the frontier's 11.89, still well below the 13.3 baseline.

reasoning.trace: The frontier (exp_0022, 11.89 over 5 seeds) changed three things at once from the col-drop-only parent (exp_0014, 12.55): it halved lr, doubled epochs (twice the compute) and added EMA at 0.999. The skill library (confounded_bundle, w=0.45) asks for two ablations. Ablation (a), EMA only at the same lr and epochs, already exists: exp_0020 scored 12.03 over 5 seeds, so EMA alone gives about -0.5. Ablation (b), lr/2 with 2x epochs and no EMA, has never been run. This run is ablation (b): it keeps column subsampling at p=0.4, group-L1 at 0 and config lr 0.0015 / 16 epochs, and removes only EMA. The idea is under-controlled (8 treatment runs, 1 control), and this control isolates the Polyak/EMA part of the shrinkage component at matched compute. If the error returns to about 12.3-12.5, EMA is the active ingredient. If it stays near 11.9, the longer low-lr schedule explains the gain and EMA is redundant. In either case the run still beats the 13.3 baseline, because column subsampling is retained.

priors: XGBoost-style column subsampling and L1 shrinkage transferred to neural BoW (arXiv:1603.02754)

votes.concern: This is a narrow ablation, not a bold move, but it is the missing control that untangles a confounded 3-way frontier change (lr/2 plus 2x epochs plus EMA). Without it, any later work built on 'shrinkage' could be credited to the wrong component, so it earns one run. The catch: exp_0020 already shows EMA alone gives about -0.5, so this run also needs 5 seeds. Otherwise a 0.4 delta can't be told apart from noise. Once the result is in, follow with a bolder step, e.g. activating the untested group-L1 shrinkage, instead of more ablations.

This is a cheap, non-redundant control. It is the missing ablation (b) for a confounded three-change bundle, and either outcome is informative. Two things could make it fragile. First, it must actually run 5 seeds to match exp_0020 and exp_0022, because single-seed noise on a ~0.4 gap would make the result uninterpretable. Second, the hypothesis frames this as 'raises err vs frontier', but nothing improves the metric directly. Its value is attribution, so budget it as a diagnostic and not as a frontier bet.

This is the one missing control in the bundle, so it is worth running. But the outcomes it must tell apart (about 11.9 vs 12.3-12.5) are within a few seed-noise widths, and the frontier and the EMA-only arm are both 5-seed means. Run this at 5 seeds too, or a single draw cannot separate the two outcomes. Interpretation is also not either/or. EMA alone already gives -0.5 and the full bundle only -0.66, so EMA and the low-lr/long schedule may be largely redundant substitutes, both acting as noise averaging. A result near 11.9 would then mean either ingredient suffices, not that EMA is inert.

doi:10.32614/r.manuals.title: R: A Language and Environment for Statistical Computing
doi:10.32614/r.manuals.summary: This introduction to R is derived from an original set of notes describing the S and S-Plus environments written in 1990-2 by Bill Venables and David M

arXiv:1506.01497.title: Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks
arXiv:1506.01497.summary: State-of-the-art object detection networks depend on region proposal algorithms to hypothesize object locations. Advances like SPPnet [1] and Fast R-CNN [2] have reduced the running time of these detection networks, exposing region proposal computation as a bottleneck. In this work, we introduce a Region Proposal Network (RPN) that shares full-image convolutional features with the detection network, thus enabling nearly cost-free region proposals. An RPN is a fully convolutional network that simultaneously predicts object bounds and objectness scores at each position. The RPN is trained end-to-end to generate high-quality region proposals, which are used by Fast R-CNN for detection. We further merge RPN and Fast R-CNN into a single network by sharing their convolutional features-using the recently popular terminology of neural networks with 'attention' mechanisms, the RPN component tells the unified network where to look. For the very deep VGG-16 model [3] , our detection system has a frame rate of 5 fps (including all steps) on a GPU, while achieving state-of-the-art object detection accuracy on PASCAL VOC 2007, 2012, and MS COCO datasets with only 300 proposals per image. In ILSVRC and COCO 2015 competitions, Faster R-CNN and RPN are the foundations of the 1st-place winning entries in several tracks. Code has been made publicly available.

arXiv:1603.02754.title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System
arXiv:1603.02754.summary: Tree boosting is a highly effective and widely used machine learning method. In this paper, we describe a scalable end-to-end tree boosting system called XGBoost, which is used widely by data scientists to achieve state-of-the-art results on many machine learning challenges. We propose a novel sparsity-aware algorithm for sparse data and weighted quantile sketch for approximate tree learning. More importantly, we provide insights on cache access patterns, data compression and sharding to build a scalable tree boosting system. By combining these insights, XGBoost scales beyond billions of examples using far fewer resources than existing systems.

doi:10.1109/5.726791.title: Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition
doi:10.1109/5.726791.summary: Multilayer neural networks trained with the back-propagation algorithm constitute the best example of a successful gradient based learning technique. Given an appropriate network architecture, gradient-based learning algorithms can be used to synthesize a complex decision surface that can classify high-dimensional patterns, such as handwritten characters, with minimal preprocessing. This paper reviews various methods applied to handwritten character recognition and compares them on a standard handwritten digit recognition task. Convolutional neural networks, which are specifically designed to deal with the variability of 2D shapes, are shown to outperform all other techniques. Real-life document recognition systems are composed of multiple modules including field extraction, segmentation recognition, and language modeling. A new learning paradigm, called graph transformer networks (GTN), allows such multimodule systems to be trained globally using gradient-based methods so as to minimize an overall performance measure. Two systems for online handwriting recognition are described. Experiments demonstrate the advantage of global training, and the flexibility of graph transformer networks. A graph transformer network for reading a bank cheque is also described. It uses convolutional neural network character recognizers combined with global training techniques to provide record accuracy on business and personal cheques. It is deployed commercially and reads several million cheques per day.

arXiv:2010.11929.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
arXiv:2010.11929.summary: While the Transformer architecture has become the de-facto standard for natural language processing tasks, its applications to computer vision remain limited. In vision, attention is either applied in conjunction with convolutional networks, or used to replace certain components of convolutional networks while keeping their overall structure in place. We show that this reliance on CNNs is not necessary and a pure transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches can perform very well on image classification tasks. When pre-trained on large amounts of data and transferred to multiple mid-sized or small image recognition benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB, etc.), Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results compared to state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train.

doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2.title: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold
doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2.summary: Abstract Proteins are essential to life, and understanding their structure can facilitate a mechanistic understanding of their function. Through an enormous experimental effort 1–4 , the structures of around 100,000 unique proteins have been determined 5 , but this represents a small fraction of the billions of known protein sequences 6,7 . Structural coverage is bottlenecked by the months to years of painstaking effort required to determine a single protein structure. Accurate computational approaches are needed to address this gap and to enable large-scale structural bioinformatics. Predicting the three-dimensional structure that a protein will adopt based solely on its amino acid sequence—the structure prediction component of the ‘protein folding problem’ 8 —has been an important open research problem for more than 50 years 9 . Despite recent progress 10–14 , existing methods fall far short of atomic accuracy, especially when no homologous structure is available. Here we provide the first computational method that can regularly predict protein structures with atomic accuracy even in cases in which no similar structure is known. We validated an entirely redesigned version of our neural network-based model, AlphaFold, in the challenging 14th Critical Assessment of protein Structure Prediction (CASP14) 15 , demonstrating accuracy competitive with experimental structures in a majority of cases and greatly outperforming other methods. Underpinning the latest version of AlphaFold is a novel machine learning approach that incorporates physical and biological knowledge about protein structure, leveraging multi-sequence alignments, into the design of the deep learning algorithm.

arXiv:2103.14030.title: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
arXiv:2103.14030.summary: This paper presents a new vision Transformer, called Swin Transformer, that capably serves as a general-purpose backbone for computer vision. Challenges in adapting Transformer from language to vision arise from differences between the two domains, such as large variations in the scale of visual entities and the high resolution of pixels in images compared to words in text. To address these differences, we propose a hierarchical Transformer whose representation is computed with Shifted windows. The shifted windowing scheme brings greater efficiency by limiting self-attention computation to non-overlapping local windows while also allowing for cross-window connection. This hierarchical architecture has the flexibility to model at various scales and has linear computational complexity with respect to image size. These qualities of Swin Transformer make it compatible with a broad range of vision tasks, including image classification (87.3 top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K) and dense prediction tasks such as object detection (58.7 box AP and 51.1 mask AP on COCO test-dev) and semantic segmentation (53.5 mIoU on ADE20K val). Its performance surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by a large margin of +2.7 box AP and +2.6 mask AP on COCO, and +3.2 mIoU on ADE20K, demonstrating the potential of Transformer-based models as vision backbones. The hierarchical design and the shifted window approach also prove beneficial for all-MLP architectures. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/Swin-Transformer.

arXiv:2303.08774.title: GPT-4 Technical Report
arXiv:2303.08774.summary: We report the development of GPT-4, a large-scale, multimodal model which can accept image and text inputs and produce text outputs. While less capable than humans in many real-world scenarios, GPT-4 exhibits human-level performance on various professional and academic benchmarks, including passing a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers. GPT-4 is a Transformer-based model pre-trained to predict the next token in a document. The post-training alignment process results in improved performance on measures of factuality and adherence to desired behavior. A core component of this project was developing infrastructure and optimization methods that behave predictably across a wide range of scales. This allowed us to accurately predict some aspects of GPT-4's performance based on models trained with no more than 1/1,000th the compute of GPT-4.

arXiv:1609.02907.title: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks
arXiv:1609.02907.summary: We present a scalable approach for semi-supervised learning on graph-structured data that is based on an efficient variant of convolutional neural networks which operate directly on graphs. We motivate the choice of our convolutional architecture via a localized first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions. Our model scales linearly in the number of graph edges and learns hidden layer representations that encode both local graph structure and features of nodes. In a number of experiments on citation networks and on a knowledge graph dataset we demonstrate that our approach outperforms related methods by a significant margin.

arXiv:1311.2524.title: Rich Feature Hierarchies for Accurate Object Detection and Semantic Segmentation
arXiv:1311.2524.summary: Object detection performance, as measured on the canonical PASCAL VOC dataset, has plateaued in the last few years. The best-performing methods are complex ensemble systems that typically combine multiple low-level image features with high-level context. In this paper, we propose a simple and scalable detection algorithm that improves mean average precision (mAP) by more than 30% relative to the previous best result on VOC 2012 -- achieving a mAP of 53.3%. Our approach combines two key insights: (1) one can apply high-capacity convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to bottom-up region proposals in order to localize and segment objects and (2) when labeled training data is scarce, supervised pre-training for an auxiliary task, followed by domain-specific fine-tuning, yields a significant performance boost. Since we combine region proposals with CNNs, we call our method R-CNN: Regions with CNN features. We also present experiments that provide insight into what the network learns, revealing a rich hierarchy of image features. Source code for the complete system is available at http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~rbg/rcnn.

arXiv:2005.14165.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
arXiv:2005.14165.summary: Recent work has demonstrated substantial gains on many NLP tasks and benchmarks by pre-training on a large corpus of text followed by fine-tuning on a specific task. While typically task-agnostic in architecture, this method still requires task-specific fine-tuning datasets of thousands or tens of thousands of examples. By contrast, humans can generally perform a new language task from only a few examples or from simple instructions - something which current NLP systems still largely struggle to do. Here we show that scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance, sometimes even reaching competitiveness with prior state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches. Specifically, we train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, 10x more than any previous non-sparse language model, and test its performance in the few-shot setting. For all tasks, GPT-3 is applied without any gradient updates or fine-tuning, with tasks and few-shot demonstrations specified purely via text interaction with the model. GPT-3 achieves strong performance on many NLP datasets, including translation, question-answering, and cloze tasks, as well as several tasks that require on-the-fly reasoning or domain adaptation, such as unscrambling words, using a novel word in a sentence, or performing 3-digit arithmetic. At the same time, we also identify some datasets where GPT-3's few-shot learning still struggles, as well as some datasets where GPT-3 faces methodological issues related to training on large web corpora. Finally, we find that GPT-3 can generate samples of news articles which human evaluators have difficulty distinguishing from articles written by humans. We discuss broader societal impacts of this finding and of GPT-3 in general.

arXiv:1704.04861.title: MobileNets: Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks for Mobile Vision Applications
arXiv:1704.04861.summary: We present a class of efficient models called MobileNets for mobile and embedded vision applications. MobileNets are based on a streamlined architecture that uses depth-wise separable convolutions to build light weight deep neural networks. We introduce two simple global hyper-parameters that efficiently trade off between latency and accuracy. These hyper-parameters allow the model builder to choose the right sized model for their application based on the constraints of the problem. We present extensive experiments on resource and accuracy tradeoffs and show strong performance compared to other popular models on ImageNet classification. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of MobileNets across a wide range of applications and use cases including object detection, finegrain classification, face attributes and large scale geo-localization.

arXiv:2407.21783.title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models
arXiv:2407.21783.summary: Modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems are powered by foundation models. This paper presents a new set of foundation models, called Llama 3. It is a herd of language models that natively support multilinguality, coding, reasoning, and tool usage. Our largest model is a dense Transformer with 405B parameters and a context window of up to 128K tokens. This paper presents an extensive empirical evaluation of Llama 3. We find that Llama 3 delivers comparable quality to leading language models such as GPT-4 on a plethora of tasks. We publicly release Llama 3, including pre-trained and post-trained versions of the 405B parameter language model and our Llama Guard 3 model for input and output safety. The paper also presents the results of experiments in which we integrate image, video, and speech capabilities into Llama 3 via a compositional approach. We observe this approach performs competitively with the state-of-the-art on image, video, and speech recognition tasks. The resulting models are not yet being broadly released as they are still under development.

arXiv:2302.13971.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
arXiv:2302.13971.summary: We introduce LLaMA, a collection of foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters. We train our models on trillions of tokens, and show that it is possible to train state-of-the-art models using publicly available datasets exclusively, without resorting to proprietary and inaccessible datasets. In particular, LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks, and LLaMA-65B is competitive with the best models, Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B. We release all our models to the research community.

arXiv:2611.14519v1.title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
arXiv:2611.14519v1.summary: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

arXiv:2611.14518v1.title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
arXiv:2611.14518v1.summary: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

arXiv:2611.14514v1.title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
arXiv:2611.14514v1.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.

arXiv:2611.14513v1.title: Online Graph Coloring: Competitive Ratios Separating Randomized and Deterministic Algorithms
arXiv:2611.14513v1.summary: We study online coloring, focusing on the competitive ratio. The best previously known results were (1) a lower bound of $Ω(n / \log^2 n)$ for both deterministic and randomized algorithms by Halldórsson and Szegedy (1994), (2) an upper bound of $O(n / \log n)$ for randomized algorithms by Halldórsson (1997), and (3) an upper bound of $O(n / \log \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms by Kawarabayashi, Yoneda, and Yoneda (2025). In this paper, we improve these results as follows: 1. A new lower bound of $Ω(n / \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms. 2. A new upper bound of $O(n (\log \log n)^2 / \log^2 n)$ for randomized algorithms. 3. A new upper bound of $O(n / (\log \log n)^{2-\varepsilon})$ for deterministic algorithms for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. For randomized algorithms, we nearly close the gap between the lower and upper bounds; the remaining gap is only $O((\log \log n)^2)$. We establish the asymptotic separation between randomized and deterministic online graph coloring. Against an oblivious adversary, a polynomial-time randomized algorithm achieves a competitive ratio asymptotically smaller than any deterministic algorithm can guarantee, even with unlimited computation.

arXiv:2611.14511v1.title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
arXiv:2611.14511v1.summary: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.

arXiv:2611.14508v1.title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
arXiv:2611.14508v1.summary: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

papers.title: R: A Language and Environment for Statistical Computing
papers.summary: This introduction to R is derived from an original set of notes describing the S and S-Plus environments written in 1990-2 by Bill Venables and David M

papers.title: Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks
papers.summary: State-of-the-art object detection networks depend on region proposal algorithms to hypothesize object locations. Advances like SPPnet [1] and Fast R-CNN [2] have reduced the running time of these detection networks, exposing region proposal computation as a bottleneck. In this work, we introduce a Region Proposal Network (RPN) that shares full-image convolutional features with the detection network, thus enabling nearly cost-free region proposals. An RPN is a fully convolutional network that simultaneously predicts object bounds and objectness scores at each position. The RPN is trained end-to-end to generate high-quality region proposals, which are used by Fast R-CNN for detection. We further merge RPN and Fast R-CNN into a single network by sharing their convolutional features-using the recently popular terminology of neural networks with 'attention' mechanisms, the RPN component tells the unified network where to look. For the very deep VGG-16 model [3] , our detection system has a frame rate of 5 fps (including all steps) on a GPU, while achieving state-of-the-art object detection accuracy on PASCAL VOC 2007, 2012, and MS COCO datasets with only 300 proposals per image. In ILSVRC and COCO 2015 competitions, Faster R-CNN and RPN are the foundations of the 1st-place winning entries in several tracks. Code has been made publicly available.

papers.title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System
papers.summary: Tree boosting is a highly effective and widely used machine learning method. In this paper, we describe a scalable end-to-end tree boosting system called XGBoost, which is used widely by data scientists to achieve state-of-the-art results on many machine learning challenges. We propose a novel sparsity-aware algorithm for sparse data and weighted quantile sketch for approximate tree learning. More importantly, we provide insights on cache access patterns, data compression and sharding to build a scalable tree boosting system. By combining these insights, XGBoost scales beyond billions of examples using far fewer resources than existing systems.

papers.title: Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition
papers.summary: Multilayer neural networks trained with the back-propagation algorithm constitute the best example of a successful gradient based learning technique. Given an appropriate network architecture, gradient-based learning algorithms can be used to synthesize a complex decision surface that can classify high-dimensional patterns, such as handwritten characters, with minimal preprocessing. This paper reviews various methods applied to handwritten character recognition and compares them on a standard handwritten digit recognition task. Convolutional neural networks, which are specifically designed to deal with the variability of 2D shapes, are shown to outperform all other techniques. Real-life document recognition systems are composed of multiple modules including field extraction, segmentation recognition, and language modeling. A new learning paradigm, called graph transformer networks (GTN), allows such multimodule systems to be trained globally using gradient-based methods so as to minimize an overall performance measure. Two systems for online handwriting recognition are described. Experiments demonstrate the advantage of global training, and the flexibility of graph transformer networks. A graph transformer network for reading a bank cheque is also described. It uses convolutional neural network character recognizers combined with global training techniques to provide record accuracy on business and personal cheques. It is deployed commercially and reads several million cheques per day.

papers.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
papers.summary: While the Transformer architecture has become the de-facto standard for natural language processing tasks, its applications to computer vision remain limited. In vision, attention is either applied in conjunction with convolutional networks, or used to replace certain components of convolutional networks while keeping their overall structure in place. We show that this reliance on CNNs is not necessary and a pure transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches can perform very well on image classification tasks. When pre-trained on large amounts of data and transferred to multiple mid-sized or small image recognition benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB, etc.), Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results compared to state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train.

papers.title: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold
papers.summary: Abstract Proteins are essential to life, and understanding their structure can facilitate a mechanistic understanding of their function. Through an enormous experimental effort 1–4 , the structures of around 100,000 unique proteins have been determined 5 , but this represents a small fraction of the billions of known protein sequences 6,7 . Structural coverage is bottlenecked by the months to years of painstaking effort required to determine a single protein structure. Accurate computational approaches are needed to address this gap and to enable large-scale structural bioinformatics. Predicting the three-dimensional structure that a protein will adopt based solely on its amino acid sequence—the structure prediction component of the ‘protein folding problem’ 8 —has been an important open research problem for more than 50 years 9 . Despite recent progress 10–14 , existing methods fall far short of atomic accuracy, especially when no homologous structure is available. Here we provide the first computational method that can regularly predict protein structures with atomic accuracy even in cases in which no similar structure is known. We validated an entirely redesigned version of our neural network-based model, AlphaFold, in the challenging 14th Critical Assessment of protein Structure Prediction (CASP14) 15 , demonstrating accuracy competitive with experimental structures in a majority of cases and greatly outperforming other methods. Underpinning the latest version of AlphaFold is a novel machine learning approach that incorporates physical and biological knowledge about protein structure, leveraging multi-sequence alignments, into the design of the deep learning algorithm.

papers.title: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
papers.summary: This paper presents a new vision Transformer, called Swin Transformer, that capably serves as a general-purpose backbone for computer vision. Challenges in adapting Transformer from language to vision arise from differences between the two domains, such as large variations in the scale of visual entities and the high resolution of pixels in images compared to words in text. To address these differences, we propose a hierarchical Transformer whose representation is computed with Shifted windows. The shifted windowing scheme brings greater efficiency by limiting self-attention computation to non-overlapping local windows while also allowing for cross-window connection. This hierarchical architecture has the flexibility to model at various scales and has linear computational complexity with respect to image size. These qualities of Swin Transformer make it compatible with a broad range of vision tasks, including image classification (87.3 top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K) and dense prediction tasks such as object detection (58.7 box AP and 51.1 mask AP on COCO test-dev) and semantic segmentation (53.5 mIoU on ADE20K val). Its performance surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by a large margin of +2.7 box AP and +2.6 mask AP on COCO, and +3.2 mIoU on ADE20K, demonstrating the potential of Transformer-based models as vision backbones. The hierarchical design and the shifted window approach also prove beneficial for all-MLP architectures. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/Swin-Transformer.

papers.title: GPT-4 Technical Report
papers.summary: We report the development of GPT-4, a large-scale, multimodal model which can accept image and text inputs and produce text outputs. While less capable than humans in many real-world scenarios, GPT-4 exhibits human-level performance on various professional and academic benchmarks, including passing a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers. GPT-4 is a Transformer-based model pre-trained to predict the next token in a document. The post-training alignment process results in improved performance on measures of factuality and adherence to desired behavior. A core component of this project was developing infrastructure and optimization methods that behave predictably across a wide range of scales. This allowed us to accurately predict some aspects of GPT-4's performance based on models trained with no more than 1/1,000th the compute of GPT-4.

papers.title: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks
papers.summary: We present a scalable approach for semi-supervised learning on graph-structured data that is based on an efficient variant of convolutional neural networks which operate directly on graphs. We motivate the choice of our convolutional architecture via a localized first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions. Our model scales linearly in the number of graph edges and learns hidden layer representations that encode both local graph structure and features of nodes. In a number of experiments on citation networks and on a knowledge graph dataset we demonstrate that our approach outperforms related methods by a significant margin.

papers.title: Rich Feature Hierarchies for Accurate Object Detection and Semantic Segmentation
papers.summary: Object detection performance, as measured on the canonical PASCAL VOC dataset, has plateaued in the last few years. The best-performing methods are complex ensemble systems that typically combine multiple low-level image features with high-level context. In this paper, we propose a simple and scalable detection algorithm that improves mean average precision (mAP) by more than 30% relative to the previous best result on VOC 2012 -- achieving a mAP of 53.3%. Our approach combines two key insights: (1) one can apply high-capacity convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to bottom-up region proposals in order to localize and segment objects and (2) when labeled training data is scarce, supervised pre-training for an auxiliary task, followed by domain-specific fine-tuning, yields a significant performance boost. Since we combine region proposals with CNNs, we call our method R-CNN: Regions with CNN features. We also present experiments that provide insight into what the network learns, revealing a rich hierarchy of image features. Source code for the complete system is available at http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~rbg/rcnn.

papers.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
papers.summary: Recent work has demonstrated substantial gains on many NLP tasks and benchmarks by pre-training on a large corpus of text followed by fine-tuning on a specific task. While typically task-agnostic in architecture, this method still requires task-specific fine-tuning datasets of thousands or tens of thousands of examples. By contrast, humans can generally perform a new language task from only a few examples or from simple instructions - something which current NLP systems still largely struggle to do. Here we show that scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance, sometimes even reaching competitiveness with prior state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches. Specifically, we train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, 10x more than any previous non-sparse language model, and test its performance in the few-shot setting. For all tasks, GPT-3 is applied without any gradient updates or fine-tuning, with tasks and few-shot demonstrations specified purely via text interaction with the model. GPT-3 achieves strong performance on many NLP datasets, including translation, question-answering, and cloze tasks, as well as several tasks that require on-the-fly reasoning or domain adaptation, such as unscrambling words, using a novel word in a sentence, or performing 3-digit arithmetic. At the same time, we also identify some datasets where GPT-3's few-shot learning still struggles, as well as some datasets where GPT-3 faces methodological issues related to training on large web corpora. Finally, we find that GPT-3 can generate samples of news articles which human evaluators have difficulty distinguishing from articles written by humans. We discuss broader societal impacts of this finding and of GPT-3 in general.

papers.title: MobileNets: Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks for Mobile Vision Applications
papers.summary: We present a class of efficient models called MobileNets for mobile and embedded vision applications. MobileNets are based on a streamlined architecture that uses depth-wise separable convolutions to build light weight deep neural networks. We introduce two simple global hyper-parameters that efficiently trade off between latency and accuracy. These hyper-parameters allow the model builder to choose the right sized model for their application based on the constraints of the problem. We present extensive experiments on resource and accuracy tradeoffs and show strong performance compared to other popular models on ImageNet classification. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of MobileNets across a wide range of applications and use cases including object detection, finegrain classification, face attributes and large scale geo-localization.

papers.title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models
papers.summary: Modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems are powered by foundation models. This paper presents a new set of foundation models, called Llama 3. It is a herd of language models that natively support multilinguality, coding, reasoning, and tool usage. Our largest model is a dense Transformer with 405B parameters and a context window of up to 128K tokens. This paper presents an extensive empirical evaluation of Llama 3. We find that Llama 3 delivers comparable quality to leading language models such as GPT-4 on a plethora of tasks. We publicly release Llama 3, including pre-trained and post-trained versions of the 405B parameter language model and our Llama Guard 3 model for input and output safety. The paper also presents the results of experiments in which we integrate image, video, and speech capabilities into Llama 3 via a compositional approach. We observe this approach performs competitively with the state-of-the-art on image, video, and speech recognition tasks. The resulting models are not yet being broadly released as they are still under development.

papers.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
papers.summary: We introduce LLaMA, a collection of foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters. We train our models on trillions of tokens, and show that it is possible to train state-of-the-art models using publicly available datasets exclusively, without resorting to proprietary and inaccessible datasets. In particular, LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks, and LLaMA-65B is competitive with the best models, Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B. We release all our models to the research community.

lit_review.json.overview: The supplied list is almost entirely off-topic for regularization of small bag-of-words text classifiers on a 10k AG News subset. None of the papers studies dropout, weight decay, label smoothing, early stopping, data augmentation, or similar regularizers for text classification under limited labels. Most entries are highly cited landmarks from other areas: vision detection and backbones, protein structure, foundation LLMs, and graph SSL. There are also 2026 preprints on unrelated subjects such as graph coloring, connectomes, and pose ranking. A few are only indirectly relevant: [arXiv:1603.02754] gives a strong regularized, sparsity-aware baseline for BoW features; [arXiv:1609.02907] offers a semi-supervised route for limited labels; [arXiv:2005.14165] is a few-shot alternative to training small models. Methodological cautions in [arXiv:2611.14508v1] and [arXiv:2611.14519v1] about under-tuned baselines are directly applicable to how regularization comparisons should be run. The colleague should treat this list as a weak evidence base. The gaps below are experiments the setting can answer, not conclusions the papers support.

themes.name: Strong non-neural baselines for sparse BoW features
themes.summary: Gradient-boosted trees with explicit L1/L2 penalties, shrinkage and column subsampling, plus sparsity-aware split finding, are a natural, heavily regularized competitor to small neural BoW classifiers. The paper benchmarks mostly tabular tasks, not text.

themes.name: Learning from limited labels via structure or pretraining
themes.summary: Two routes are represented. Graph-based semi-supervised propagation [arXiv:1609.02907] leverages unlabelled neighbours. Large-scale pretraining, then transfer or few-shot use, appears in [arXiv:2005.14165], [arXiv:1311.2524], [arXiv:2010.11929], [arXiv:2302.13971], [arXiv:2407.21783] and [arXiv:2303.08774]. These treat pretraining as the main regularizer when labels are scarce, but none isolates it against classic regularizers for small models.

themes.name: Fair comparison and tuning-budget methodology
themes.summary: These papers warn that comparisons are biased when baselines are under-tuned or inherit hyperparameters tuned on the favoured model [arXiv:2611.14508v1]. [arXiv:2611.14519v1] makes the same point about single, unjustified task-specific baselines and about how much of a model to adapt (from bias-only tuning to full fine-tuning). Both apply directly to regularization ablations.

themes.name: Architecture and capacity control
themes.summary: Capacity reduction through architecture is a form of implicit regularization. Examples are width multipliers [arXiv:1704.04861] and convolutional weight sharing [doi:10.1109/5.726791]. All evidence is from vision.

themes.name: Off-topic entries
themes.summary: These papers have no bearing on text classifier regularization.

paper_notes.contribution: Regularized boosting objective (L1/L2 on leaf weights, shrinkage, subsampling) with sparsity-aware splits suited to high-dimensional sparse inputs like BoW.
paper_notes.limitation: No text-classification or low-label experiments; whether it beats a tuned linear or MLP BoW model on 10k AG News is untested here.

paper_notes.contribution: Semi-supervised node classification by propagating features over a graph, effective with very few labels.
paper_notes.limitation: It requires a graph, such as a document kNN or word co-occurrence graph, which AG News does not provide. Results are on citation networks, not news topics.

paper_notes.contribution: Shows scale enables few-shot classification without gradient updates, an alternative to training regularized small models.
paper_notes.limitation: Compute cost is incomparable to a small BoW model. It gives no evidence about what regularizes small models trained from scratch.

paper_notes.contribution: Formalizes three tuning estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 constrained by independent data (P3). It shows how tuning on the favoured model biases comparisons.
paper_notes.limitation: Its domain is neuroscience, and it gives no empirical ML regularization results. The transfer to ML ablations is by analogy.

paper_notes.contribution: Compares adaptation depths (bias-only through full fine-tuning) against from-scratch baselines with justified configurations.
paper_notes.limitation: It covers medical segmentation only, not text or BoW.

paper_notes.contribution: Global width and resolution multipliers trade capacity against accuracy.
paper_notes.limitation: The evidence is from vision. Width as a regularizer for small-data text MLPs is not studied.

paper_notes.contribution: Shows architectural priors (weight sharing) reduce effective capacity and improve generalization.
paper_notes.limitation: Its BoW inputs discard word order, so convolutional priors do not carry over directly.

gaps.gap: Does a fully tuned regularized linear model (logistic regression with L2 or L1 on TF-IDF BoW) match or beat a small MLP on val_top1_err on the 10k AG News subset? The test is to give each model its own hyperparameter search with an equal trial budget.
gaps.why_open: No listed paper evaluates this setting. [arXiv:2611.14508v1] and [arXiv:2611.14519v1] show that comparisons under unequal tuning are biased, so any claimed regularization gain needs per-model tuning (the P2 estimand).

gaps.gap: Gradient-boosted trees versus neural BoW classifiers at 10k labels, comparing XGBoost's L1/L2 and subsampling regularizers against dropout and weight decay.
gaps.why_open: [arXiv:1603.02754] claims strength on sparse data but reports no text-classification benchmarks.

gaps.gap: Whether a kNN document graph built over the full AG News training pool, with labels only on the 10k subset, lowers error relative to supervised-only regularization when used for graph propagation.
gaps.why_open: [arXiv:1609.02907] needs a given graph. How much a constructed similarity graph helps over dropout or weight decay alone has not been measured for BoW text.

gaps.gap: Interaction of explicit regularizers (dropout, weight decay, label smoothing, early stopping) with model width in small BoW MLPs. Do they substitute for each other or stack?
gaps.why_open: Width-as-capacity is studied only in vision [arXiv:1704.04861]. No listed paper crosses width with explicit regularizers on text.

gaps.gap: Cost-matched comparison: a frozen pretrained embedding or LLM few-shot baseline versus a from-scratch regularized BoW model at equal labelled data.
gaps.why_open: [arXiv:2005.14165] and [arXiv:2302.13971] imply pretraining dominates, but they never compare against a properly regularized small model under compute or latency constraints.

trends: Pretraining at scale is increasingly treated as the default answer to label scarcity, displacing explicit regularization research ([arXiv:2005.14165], [arXiv:2407.21783]).
Growing scrutiny of baseline tuning and fair comparisons ([arXiv:2611.14508v1], [arXiv:2611.14519v1]).
Partial or parameter-efficient adaptation (for example bias-only tuning) as an implicit regularizer ([arXiv:2611.14519v1]).
The supplied corpus contains almost no direct work on small text-classifier regularization, so the relevant literature must be gathered elsewhere.

"""FROZEN module for the agnews-bow engine: data, model construction, and evaluation.
Never edit this file. It is the trust anchor:

  1. `load_train()` hands the agent ONLY the training folds; val and test never leave here.
  2. `build_model()` is frozen, so the model the scorer reconstructs is defined by trusted code.
     The agent shapes it through hyperparameters and changes the training procedure in train.py.
  3. `score(artifact)` loads a state_dict with `weights_only=True` into the frozen architecture,
     evaluates on a frozen split, and emits the trusted number from pristine ROOT.

Data: a fixed, class-stratified subset of AG News (Zhang et al., 2015): 8,000 training-split
articles as the cross-validation pool and 2,000 official-test articles as the held-out test.
Text is lower-cased, split on non-alphanumerics, truncated to 64 tokens and hashed into 20,000
buckets (id 0 is padding). The subset is built once from the Hugging Face copy and cached.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import re
import sys
import zlib
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

METRIC_NAME = "val_top1_err"
N_FOLDS = 5
N_CLASSES = 4
VOCAB = 20000          # hash buckets; token ids are 1..VOCAB, 0 pads
MAX_LEN = 64
_POOL, _TEST = 8000, 2000
_DATASET = "fancyzhx/ag_news"
_TOKEN = re.compile(r"[a-z0-9]+")
_cache: dict = {}


def encode(text: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """Hashed token ids for one text, padded to MAX_LEN. Stable across processes (crc32)."""
    ids = [zlib.crc32(t.encode()) % VOCAB + 1 for t in _TOKEN.findall(text.lower())[:MAX_LEN]]
    return np.array(ids + [0] * (MAX_LEN - len(ids)), dtype="int64")


def _data_path() -> Path:
    root = os.environ.get("SCHOLARLOOP_DATA_DIR") or Path.home() / ".cache" / "scholarloop"
    return Path(root) / "agnews-bow-v1.npz"


def _stratified(labels: np.ndarray, n: int, seed: int) -> np.ndarray:
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    per = n // N_CLASSES
    return np.sort(np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(labels == c), per, replace=False)
                                   for c in range(N_CLASSES)]))


def _build(path: Path) -> None:
    from datasets import load_dataset   # only needed the first time; the subset is cached after

    raw = load_dataset(_DATASET)
    out = {}
    for name, split, n in (("pool", "train", _POOL), ("test", "test", _TEST)):
        labels = np.array(raw[split]["label"], dtype="int64")
        keep = _stratified(labels, n, seed=0)
        texts = raw[split].select(keep.tolist())["text"]
        out[f"x_{name}"] = np.stack([encode(t) for t in texts])
        out[f"y_{name}"] = labels[keep]
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    tmp = path.with_suffix(".tmp.npz")
    np.savez_compressed(tmp, **out)
    os.replace(tmp, path)


def _arrays() -> dict:
    if not _cache:
        path = _data_path()
        if not path.exists():
            _build(path)
        with np.load(path) as data:
            _cache.update({k: data[k] for k in data.files})
    return _cache


def _split(fold: int = 0):
    """Train / val / held-out test. The pool is cut into N_FOLDS stratified folds: `fold` is the
    val split the loop selects on, the rest is training data. The test split is scored only on
    full-tier runs and never selected on."""
    from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold

    d = _arrays()
    folds = list(StratifiedKFold(N_FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=0).split(d["x_pool"], d["y_pool"]))
    tr, va = folds[fold]
    return d["x_pool"][tr], d["x_pool"][va], d["x_test"], d["y_pool"][tr], d["y_pool"][va], d["y_test"]


def _fold_from_env() -> int:
    return int(os.environ.get("SCHOLARLOOP_FOLD", "0"))


def load_train():
    """Training data only: (token ids [N, MAX_LEN] with 0 as padding, labels [N])."""
    x_tr, _x_val, _x_te, y_tr, _y_val, _y_te = _split(_fold_from_env())
    return x_tr, y_tr


def build_model(hparams: dict):
    """Frozen architecture: mean of token embeddings (padding masked) → `depth` hidden layers of
    width `hidden` → class logits. `embed_dim`, `hidden` and `depth` are hyperparameters."""
    import torch
    import torch.nn as nn

    class BagOfEmbeddings(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self, dim: int, hidden: int, depth: int):
            super().__init__()
            self.embed = nn.Embedding(VOCAB + 1, dim, padding_idx=0)
            layers, d = [], dim
            for _ in range(depth):
                layers += [nn.Linear(d, hidden), nn.ReLU()]
                d = hidden
            self.head = nn.Sequential(*layers, nn.Linear(d, N_CLASSES))

        def pool(self, ids):
            mask = (ids != 0).unsqueeze(-1).to(self.embed.weight.dtype)
            return (self.embed(ids) * mask).sum(1) / mask.sum(1).clamp(min=1.0)

        def forward(self, ids):
            return self.head(self.pool(ids))

    torch.manual_seed(0)    # construction is deterministic; train.py reseeds before initialising
    return BagOfEmbeddings(int(hparams["embed_dim"]), int(hparams["hidden"]), int(hparams["depth"]))


def evaluate(model, split: str = "val", fold: int = 0) -> float:
    """Top-1 error (%) on a frozen split (val fold `fold`, or the held-out test). Lower is better."""
    import torch

    _x_tr, x_val, x_te, _y_tr, y_val, y_te = _split(fold)
    x, y = (x_te, y_te) if split == "test" else (x_val, y_val)
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        pred = model(torch.from_numpy(x)).argmax(1).numpy()
    return round(float((pred != y).mean() * 100.0), 4)


def emit_result(value: float, seeds: list[float] | None = None, config: dict | None = None) -> None:
    print("SCHOLARLOOP_RESULT " + json.dumps(
        {"metric_name": METRIC_NAME, "value": float(value),
         "seeds": seeds or [value], "config": config or {}}))


def score(artifact_path: str, split: str = "val", fold: int = 0) -> None:
    """Trusted metric: rebuild the frozen model from config, load the agent's weights (safely),
    and score on a frozen split."""
    import torch

    bundle = torch.load(artifact_path, weights_only=True)   # state_dict only, no code execution
    cfg = bundle["config"]
    model = build_model(cfg)
    model.load_state_dict(bundle["state_dict"])
    emit_result(evaluate(model, split, fold), config=cfg)


def parse_score_args(argv: list[str]):
    """`score <artifact> [val|test] [fold]` -> (artifact, split, fold), or None if malformed."""
    if not 2 <= len(argv) <= 4 or argv[0] != "score":
        return None
    split = argv[2] if len(argv) > 2 else "val"
    fold = argv[3] if len(argv) > 3 else "0"
    if split not in ("val", "test") or not fold.isdigit() or int(fold) >= N_FOLDS:
        return None
    return argv[1], split, int(fold)


def _main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    parsed = parse_score_args(argv)
    if parsed is None:
        print("usage: python -m engines.text_cls.prepare score <artifact> [test | val [fold]]",
              file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    score(*parsed)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(_main(sys.argv[1:]))

"""EDITABLE training script for the agnews-bow engine.

Treatment: XGBoost-style column subsampling (per-step vocabulary-id dropout) plus
group-L1 shrinkage on embedding rows. Artifact interface unchanged.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from engines.text_cls import prepare

HPARAMS = {
    "lr": 0.003,
    "embed_dim": 64,
    "hidden": 64,
    "depth": 1,
    "weight_decay": 0.0001,
    "epochs": 8,
}
BATCH = 128
COL_DROP = 0.25      # fraction of vocabulary columns dropped per step
GROUP_L1 = 1e-5      # coefficient on sum of embedding-row L2 norms


def effective_hparams() -> dict:
    return {**HPARAMS, **json.loads(os.environ.get("SCHOLARLOOP_CONFIG", "{}"))}


def column_subsample(ids: torch.Tensor, vocab: int, p: float) -> torch.Tensor:
    if p <= 0:
        return ids
    keep = torch.rand(vocab) >= p
    keep[0] = True
    masked = torch.where(keep[ids], ids, torch.zeros_like(ids))
    empty = (masked != 0).sum(dim=1) == 0
    if empty.any():
        masked[empty] = ids[empty]
    return masked


def group_l1(weight: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    w = weight[1:]
    return torch.sqrt((w * w).sum(dim=1) + 1e-12).sum()


def train_model(seed: int, h: dict) -> nn.Module:
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    x_tr, y_tr = prepare.load_train()           # training folds only, no val leakage
    model = prepare.build_model(h)              # frozen architecture, shaped by hparams
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    for p in model.parameters():                # seed-dependent initialisation
        if p.dim() > 1:
            nn.init.normal_(p, std=0.1)
    with torch.no_grad():
        model.embed.weight[0].zero_()
    vocab = model.embed.num_embeddings
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=float(h["lr"]), weight_decay=float(h["weight_decay"]))
    loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    xt, yt = torch.from_numpy(x_tr), torch.from_numpy(y_tr)
    model.train()
    for _ in range(int(h["epochs"])):
        order = torch.randperm(len(xt))
        for i in range(0, len(order), BATCH):
            idx = order[i:i + BATCH]
            xb = column_subsample(xt[idx], vocab, COL_DROP)
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yt[idx])
            if GROUP_L1 > 0:
                loss = loss + GROUP_L1 * group_l1(model.embed.weight)
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
    return model


def main() -> None:
    seed = int(os.environ.get("SCHOLARLOOP_SEED", "0"))
    h = effective_hparams()
    model = train_model(seed, h)
    torch.save({"config": h, "state_dict": dict(model.state_dict())},
               os.environ["SCHOLARLOOP_ARTIFACT"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""EDITABLE training script for the agnews-bow engine (XGBoost-style regularizers).

Column subsampling -> per-step vocabulary-column dropout (masked ids mapped to padding 0).
Leaf L1 -> group-L1 on embedding rows. Shrinkage -> low lr, many epochs, EMA weight averaging.
Saves EMA state_dict + config to $SCHOLARLOOP_ARTIFACT; scoring is done by the frozen runner.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from engines.text_cls import prepare

HPARAMS = {
    "lr": 0.003,
    "embed_dim": 64,
    "hidden": 64,
    "depth": 1,
    "weight_decay": 0.0001,
    "epochs": 8,
}
BATCH = 128
COL_DROP = 0.3
GROUP_L1 = 1e-5
EMA_DECAY = 0.999


def effective_hparams() -> dict:
    return {**HPARAMS, **json.loads(os.environ.get("SCHOLARLOOP_CONFIG", "{}"))}


def train_model(seed: int, h: dict) -> nn.Module:
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    x_tr, y_tr = prepare.load_train()
    model = prepare.build_model(h)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    for p in model.parameters():
        if p.dim() > 1:
            nn.init.normal_(p, std=0.1)
    with torch.no_grad():
        model.embed.weight[0].zero_()
    vocab = model.embed.weight.shape[0]
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=float(h["lr"]), weight_decay=float(h["weight_decay"]))
    loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    xt, yt = torch.from_numpy(x_tr).long(), torch.from_numpy(y_tr)
    ema = {k: v.detach().clone() for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}
    model.train()
    for _ in range(int(h["epochs"])):
        order = torch.randperm(len(xt))
        for i in range(0, len(order), BATCH):
            idx = order[i:i + BATCH]
            ids = xt[idx]
            if COL_DROP > 0:
                keep = (torch.rand(vocab) >= COL_DROP).long()
                keep[0] = 1
                ids = ids * keep[ids]
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss = loss_fn(model(ids), yt[idx])
            if GROUP_L1 > 0:
                w = model.embed.weight[1:]
                loss = loss + GROUP_L1 * torch.sqrt((w * w).sum(dim=1) + 1e-12).sum()
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
            with torch.no_grad():
                for k, v in model.state_dict().items():
                    if v.dtype.is_floating_point:
                        ema[k].mul_(EMA_DECAY).add_(v.detach(), alpha=1.0 - EMA_DECAY)
                    else:
                        ema[k].copy_(v)
    model.load_state_dict(ema)
    with torch.no_grad():
        model.embed.weight[0].zero_()
    return model

    seed = int(os.environ.get("SCHOLARLOOP_SEED", "0"))
    h = effective_hparams()
    model = train_model(seed, h)
    torch.save({"config": h, "state_dict": dict(model.state_dict())},
               os.environ["SCHOLARLOOP_ARTIFACT"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

  2. `build_model()` is frozen, so the model the scorer reconstructs is defined by trusted code.
